The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,2,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,0,-1⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,-1)-f(0,2,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,0,-1⟩-⟨0,2,1⟩) \\ 2-(-7) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,-4y,2z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},-4{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}9 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =⟨2{c}_{1},-4{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =2{c}_{1}+8{c}_{2}-4{c}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-2}{(-2)}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ x & =-\frac{y-2}{2}=-\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t,\,\,y=2-2t,\,z=1-2t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t,\,\,{c}_{2}=2-2t,\,{c}_{3}=1-2t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $2{c}_{1}+8{c}_{2}-4{c}_{3}=9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(t)+8(2-2t)-4(1-2t) & =9 \\ 2t+16-16t-4+8t & =9 \\ -6t & =-3 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =2-2(\frac{1}{2})=1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-2(\frac{1}{2})=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(\frac{1}{2},1,0).$
